Sampling can change model rankings; these challenges measure sensitivity to candidate construction, not full-catalog accuracy ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Recommended reproducibility specification: count training interactions per item separately within each category; reserve a zero-count bin and define deciles over positive-count catalog items, publishing boundaries and keeping equal counts together. Define popularity-matched as uniform sampling within the validation target’s bin; distinguish this from sampling proportional to popularity. Document the baseline training sampler’s exact distribution and exclusions. Use identical eligible catalogs across challenges: exclude padding, observed history and the validation target, without accessing hidden test interactions. Draw 99 distinct distractors without replacement. Specify sparse-bin expansion by nearest log-count distance, breaking ties by item ID; report expansion rates. Save candidate IDs and use stable seeds keyed by category, user, challenge and replicate.

For semantic distractors, freeze title-plus-description preprocessing, vocabulary, IDF corpus and vectorizer settings; use L2-normalized TF-IDF cosine ([scikit-learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/metrics.html)). Specify the reference explicitly: the last observed history item measures contextual similarity; the validation target measures target confusability. Report these separately. Select highest-similarity eligible items, resolving equal similarities by item ID. Treat empty or zero-vector text as unavailable; backfill from the popularity-matched pool and report fallback rates. Resolve model-score ties consistently across challenges.

To isolate semantic difficulty, compare similar versus random candidates within identical popularity-bin quotas and metadata-covered pools; additionally match text length and title/description availability. Report common-user paired differences, repeated candidate draws, coverage strata and popularity-only/text-only baselines. Distractor relevance remains unknown: semantic neighbors may be valid alternatives. Describe rank changes as confusability sensitivity, not proof of preference errors; candidate selection itself interacts with popularity bias ([Ihemelandu and Ekstrand](https://mdw.ekstrandom.net/pubs/wi-sampled-eval)).
